analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to publicly report how many claims they deny and why.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require health plans to disclose their claim denial numbers and reasons in annual reports, was introduced in July 2026 and has been sitting in committee with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Labor Department to write a rule requiring employer-based health plans to report, in their annual filings, how many claims they receive, approve, deny, and how many denials get reversed on appeal. Plans would have to break this down by type of care — urgent care, hospital stays, prescription drugs, mental health, cancer treatment — and state why claims were denied, such as medical necessity or missing prior authorization. It also requires plans to disclose how often they use artificial intelligence or automated tools to process claims [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families covered by employer health plans gain visibility into how often their plan denies care and why — data that today is largely hidden from the public. Regulators, journalists, and patient advocates could compare plans' denial rates, spot plans that deny unusually often, and see whether automated systems are driving denials. People in small employer plans benefit specifically because the bill extends reporting duties to plans with fewer than 100 participants, which currently file only simplified reports [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires every group health plan to disclose annually how many claims it submitted, approved, denied, and reversed on appeal — numbers patients currently cannot see for their own plan [S2].

Forces plans to state why claims were denied — medical necessity, lack of prior authorization, excluded services, administrative reasons — so patterns of improper denials become visible rather than invisible [S2].

Requires disclosure of how many claims were processed with artificial intelligence or other automated decision-making tools, and how many of those were paid versus denied, as insurers' use of AI to deny claims has become a public concern [S2].
Closes a gap for workers at small employers by requiring plans with fewer than 100 participants to file the full report instead of the simplified version currently allowed [S2].

Includes dollar totals for claims paid and denied and counts claims that were not decided within the required time frame, giving regulators a measure of how well plans follow their own appeal deadlines [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group health plans bear the cost of collecting, categorizing, and reporting this data each year — a real but modest compliance burden, since plans already must adjudicate and track this information internally under existing claim-procedure rules [S2]. If the resulting public data embarrasses plans with high denial rates, they could face reputational and regulatory pressure, and might respond by pricing that risk into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone changes nothing directly: the bill creates no new right to appeal, no limit on denials, and no penalty for denying claims — a plan can report a high denial rate and keep denying [S2].
The bill expands annual reporting to plans with fewer than 100 participants, imposing new administrative costs on small employers who currently qualify for simplified reporting [S2].
Plans with 20 or fewer claims in a category (drugs, mental health, or cancer) are exempt from reporting that category's numbers, so the picture will be incomplete for small plans [S2].
The Labor Department has one year to write the regulation, and the value of the data depends entirely on how detailed that rule turns out to be and whether the department enforces it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: public denial-rate data would let workers compare plans, let regulators target enforcement, and let advocates document practices like AI-driven denials — all without any new mandate on care itself. The costs are compliance work for plans and some new paperwork for small employers. As a transparency measure it is well-targeted but modest; by itself it does not stop a single denial, and its practical value rests on a future regulation being written strictly and enforced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2026 and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat ever since with no cosponsors and no hearings or votes.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the Health Claim Denial Transparency Act on July 16, 2026 [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which is the standard first step — the committee decides whether the bill ever gets considered [S1].
No other action has been taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no members have signed on as cosponsors [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained — the bill has simply gone nowhere. Health insurers and employer plans are unaffected because the reporting requirement has not advanced, and workers' plans are no more transparent than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, for now, as the bill sits untouched

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; no cosponsors have joined

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no cosponsors have signed on, so no partisan pattern exists yet — the only recorded action is the Democratic sponsor's introduction and the committee's inaction.

industries.note: The bill forces them to publish their own denial numbers, denial reasons, and AI usage each year. It bans nothing, but it exposes the denial practices that generate savings for plans and frustrate patients, and it invites regulators and the public to compare plans.

Most employer plans must now produce detailed denial reports annually, including small plans under 100 participants that currently file only simplified reports. Employers also benefit as plan buyers, since comparable denial data makes it easier to judge which insurers are actually delivering care versus denying it.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee activity more than two weeks after introduction. Most bills at this stage — referred to committee, no hearing scheduled, no cosponsors — die quietly at the end of the Congress. It would need the committee to schedule a markup and other members, ideally from both parties, to sign on before it has any realistic path to a floor vote.
